items.q: Match the following classification to its example — 1) Type 1 2) Type 2 3) Gestational 4) Other specific types … A) Autoimmune β-cell destruction B) Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency C) Onset in pregnancy D) Monogenic, drug-induced, pancreatic disease
items.exp: Type 1 is autoimmune β-cell destruction; Type 2 is insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency; GDM is diagnosed in pregnancy; 'other specific types' include monogenic, drug-induced and pancreatic diabetes. (Book p919)

items.q: A 12-year-old presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and DKA. Anti-GAD is positive. The diagnosis is:
items.exp: Children with DKA and positive GAD have autoimmune Type 1 diabetes, not Type 2 or MODY. (Book p919)

items.q: Assess classification: I Type 2 diabetes is the most common form worldwide. II Latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA) is a slow Type 1 variant.
items.exp: Type 2 is the most common form; LADA is autoimmune diabetes in adults that is initially non-insulin requiring but slowly progresses. (Book p919)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a 'dirty dozen' cause of secondary diabetes?
items.exp: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is associated with autoimmune diabetes (Type 1-like), not classical secondary 'dirty dozen' causes like pancreatitis, Cushing or steroids. (Book p919)

items.q: Monogenic diabetes caused by HNF1A mutations and responsive to low-dose sulfonylureas is also known as ___.
items.exp: MODY 3 (HNF1A) is the classic sulfonylurea-responsive monogenic diabetes; MODY 2 (GCK) is typically diet-controlled. (Book p919)

items.q: Match the following MODY subtype to its key feature — 1) HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) 2) GCK-MODY (MODY 2) 3) HNF4A-MODY (MODY 1) … A) Sulfonylurea-responsive, progressive B) Mild stable hyperglycaemia, often no Rx C) Macrosomia + neonatal hypoglycaemia then diabetes
items.exp: HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) is sulfonylurea-responsive and progressive; GCK-MODY (MODY 2) is mild and usually not treated; HNF4A-MODY is associated with macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia. (Book p919)

items.q: A 24-year-old with mild fasting hyperglycaemia and a family history of 'mild diabetes' across three generations has HbA1c 6.0%. Genetic testing is most likely to find:
items.exp: Mild stable hyperglycaemia across generations fits GCK-MODY (MODY 2); HNF1A-MODY is progressive and typically requires treatment. (Book p919)

items.q: Assess autoimmune screening: I GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 antibodies classify autoimmune diabetes. II Antibody-negative autoimmune diabetes is impossible.
items.exp: GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 are the principal autoantibodies; a small subset of autoimmune diabetes is antibody-negative (so-called idiopathic Type 1). (Book p919)

items.q: Match the following test to its role — 1) Fasting glucose 2) 2-hour OGTT 3) HbA1c 4) C-peptide … A) Screening and diagnosis B) Sensitive for IGT C) Reflects chronic glycemia D) Endogenous insulin secretion
items.exp: Fasting glucose is the workhorse screening test; OGTT is most sensitive for IGT; HbA1c reflects chronic glycemia; C-peptide reflects endogenous insulin secretion. (Book p919)

items.q: A 50-year-old has fasting glucose 105 mg/dL but 2-hour post-load 168 mg/dL. The most consistent label is:
items.exp: 2-hour glucose 140–199 with normal FPG is isolated IGT. (Book p919)

items.q: The diagnostic 75-g OGTT detects ___ more sensitively than fasting glucose.
items.exp: The 75-g OGTT detects IGT earlier than fasting glucose. (Book p919)

items.q: Assess fructosamine and 1,5-AG: I They reflect shorter-term glycemia than HbA1c. II They are useful when HbA1c is unreliable.
items.exp: Fructosamine and 1,5-AG reflect 2–3 weeks of glycemia, useful in pregnancy or haemoglobinopathies where HbA1c is unreliable. (Book p919)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a test that does NOT assess chronic glycaemia?
items.exp: Random plasma glucose is a snapshot; HbA1c, fructosamine and 1,5-AG all integrate glycaemia over different windows. (Book p919)
